r: A vaccine lets the body practice fighting an infection without the deadly outcome. It delivers fragments of the pathogen, called antigens, which can come from inactivated virus particles, purified protein pieces, or mRNA that muscle cells in the shoulder turn into protein. These fragments travel to lymph nodes, where dendritic cells pick them up and show peptides on MHC molecules. Helper T cells, chosen from billions of randomly generated receptor variants because they match the epitope, signal B cells to multiply inside germinal centers. There, over two to four weeks, antibody-producing cells mutate and improve how tightly they bind. Most effector cells then die, but long-lived plasma cells and memory lymphocytes last for years, sometimes decades. Immunologists know the benefit comes later. When the real pathogen arrives, the secondary response starts within days, not the week or more of the first response, and often stops the pathogen before symptoms appear. Aluminum-salt adjuvants, used since the 1930s, strengthen the alarm signal. Boosters repeat the lesson, and immunity strengthens.
